name: Elena Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hartley's, a family builder out in the farming country, eight of us. We put up houses, barns and machine sheds, and in winter we do repairs, roofs mostly, sometimes the church. I'm a carpenter, same as my dad was, and I did my apprenticeship with him before he passed it on to Hartley's. I'm in the yard by seven, load the timber, and we're usually on site by half past with the radio on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I value that you can stand back and see what you made. I re-hung the main door on St Michael's three winters ago, and every Sunday I walk through it and nobody knows but me and God. What's hard is the pay, it's never been much out here, and there's only Hartley's and one other firm within the hour. Mark drives a delivery lorry, and with the two kids and the mortgage we've got a few weeks' money at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these big tech people promise the moon every few years. Good honest work is still good honest work. I'd say that at the yard and after church, I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I've never used one of those AI programs and I don't intend to start. If the world stays as it is, I can carry on doing what my dad taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working for Hartley's, keep the family going, keep the Sunday routine. If Hartley wants a computer for the books, that's his decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really, that some things stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your dad a few times. What would he have said about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have said 'can it plane a door?' and then gone back to his tea. He didn't trust anything that hadn't been tested by weather. I'm the same, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that bothers you, even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones don't want to come into the trade. Hartley hasn't had an apprentice in four years. That worries me far more than any computer.

S0.say: She isn't surprised, since big tech promises the moon every few years, and good honest work is still good honest work. She'd say it at the yard and after church, not online.
S0.think: She'd be glad: she's never used AI programs and doesn't intend to. If the world stays the same, she can keep doing what her father taught her.
S0.do: Keeps working for Hartley's, keeps the family and Sunday routine going, and leaves any computer bookkeeping to her boss.
S0.feel: Calm and grateful that some things stay the same.
S0.quote: He'd have said 'can it plane a door?' and then gone back to his tea.
S0.fieldNote: Elena's identity is woven from her father's trade, her church and her rural community. She distrusts tech companies more than technology itself. Her standing worry is the lack of young apprentices, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but businesses have the right to use what they want. People should be helped to learn a new trade, through apprenticeships, not handouts. And families should look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about Mark more than me. Lorries driving themselves is what they always talk about, and his job's the one I'd watch. Hartley's won't be buying robots any time soon, we still use a pencil and a tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first. I'd keep working and try to put a little aside, maybe twenty a week, because Mark's job might change. I'd push Josef towards a trade when he's older, a proper apprenticeship like I had, and I'd ask Hartley to take one on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not me, really, it's the house as a whole I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'families should look after their own'. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother has a farm twenty minutes away. If Mark lost his job, he could help out there for a while, and my mum would help with the children. That's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I'm not good with screens and I don't trust them. If a machine came on site, I'd let the young ones work it and I'd do what it can't.

S1.say: It's a shame, but businesses have the right to use what they want. People should be helped into a new trade through apprenticeships, not handouts, and families should look after their own.
S1.think: She worries more about her partner's lorry-driving job than her own, since self-driving lorries are always mentioned. Her small firm still uses a pencil and tape.
S1.do: Keeps working, saves about twenty a week in case her partner's job changes, and steers her son towards a proper apprenticeship while asking her boss to take one on.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about the household rather than her own job.
S1.quote: Hartley's won't be buying robots any time soon, we still use a pencil and a tape.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is about the household's second income, not her own trade. She relies on family, her brother's farm and her mother, rather than the state. She'd leave new machines to younger workers rather than learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast, and the big tech companies should be held responsible for the damage they cause. People need work, not just a cheque in the post. I'd say we need to look after our own communities, because no one in the city is going to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years would frighten me. If robots can do my job and Mark's at the same time, we'd be in real trouble, with only a few weeks of money. I'd pray, I'll be honest, and I'd lean on family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That first month we'd cut everything, no meals out, no holiday, the kids' activities would stop. I'd ask my brother if Mark or I could work on the farm for a while, and I'd take any odd repair job from neighbours for cash. I'd keep going to Hartley's as long as there's work, and I'd ask the church about the food bank if it came to that, though it would hurt my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not panicking, I have my faith, but I'd lie awake and pray more than I've ever done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use those two years before it arrives for anything in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save every penny, and do every bit of extra work I can get. I'm not going to learn computers at forty-three, so I'd make hay while the sun shines. And I'd make sure the children don't know how worried we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it would hurt your pride to use the food bank. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family has always been the ones giving, not taking. My dad used to drop off logs to the older folk every winter. Going to the church for help would feel like the world had turned upside down.

S2.say: It's going too fast and big tech companies should be held responsible for the damage. People need work, not just a cheque, and communities must look after their own because no one in the city will.
S2.think: Two years would frighten her: if robots take both her job and Mark's at once, they'd be in real trouble with only weeks of money. She'd pray and lean on family.
S2.do: Cuts meals out, holidays and the children's activities, and asks her brother for farm work for her or Mark. Takes cash repair jobs from neighbours, keeps working at Hartley's and would reluctantly turn to the church food bank if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened and sleepless, but held back from panic by her faith.
S2.quote: My family has always been the ones giving, not taking.
S2.fieldNote: Her faith steadies her, but the risk to both incomes at once makes this a real threat. She'd turn to family and church before the state, and would find that hard. She has no intention of learning computers even under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get young people into apprenticeships for whatever work is left, and to keep businesses local. The government should help with training, but people should stand on their own feet. I'd say it at the parish meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years would hit Mark first. Lorries would go before barn roofs. So we'd have a few years where I'm still working but his money's gone, and I don't know how we'd manage on just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard straight away, even if it means no holidays for five years. I'd look at getting more cash repair work on the side, because farmers always need something fixing. I'd sit tight with Hartley's and see what happens rather than jump into something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, more than the slow worry I had with the lighter change. It's the thought of both of us going, one after the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, it all comes at once and we're sunk. With five, it comes in pieces, Mark first, then me. That's a bit better, but it's like watching the water rise one step at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about learning the new tools, with five years to do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if Hartley's brought something in and showed me on site. But I'm not going to a college to sit in front of a screen. I learn with my hands, always have.

S3.say: Five years is time to get young people into apprenticeships and keep businesses local. Government should help with training, but people should stand on their own feet; she'd say so at the parish meeting.
S3.think: She expects Mark's lorry job to go first, leaving a few years with only her income, and she doesn't know how they'd manage on that alone.
S3.do: Saves hard at once, giving up holidays, and builds cash repair work for local farmers. Sits tight at Hartley's to see what happens rather than jumping into something unfamiliar.
S3.feel: Alarmed at the thought of both incomes going one after the other.
S3.quote: That's a bit better, but it's like watching the water rise one step at a time.
S3.fieldNote: For Elena, more time mainly changes the order in which the household's incomes disappear. She'd consider learning tools only if shown on site by her own firm. Her politics are local and parish-based, favouring apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to look after our own, train the young ones and keep the community together. I wouldn't want a big government scheme, I'd want proper apprenticeships and local firms supported. And I'd say families need to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years still worries me, but I could see us getting through. Mark could look for something else in the first few years, and by the end Hannah would be at work and Josef nearly. I'd be fifty-three, and I'd hope there's still some old church that needs a carpenter who knows what she's doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily, put something extra on the mortgage when I can, and keep working for Hartley's. I'd talk to Mark about him finding something safer in the next couple of years. And I'd push Hannah and Josef towards work that needs a person, nursing, farming, a trade, whatever they're good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Ten years feels like time to put things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah and Josef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that work is good for you, whatever it is, and to learn something useful with their hands or their hearts. Hannah wants to be a nurse, I'd say go for it. Josef likes helping his uncle with the cows, maybe that's his path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your own work, given a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe learn a bit more of the restoration side, old timber frames and church roofs, because that's where they'll still want a person. But I'd learn it from an old craftsman, not a computer. That's how my dad learned and that's how I'd do it.

S4.say: Ten years is time to look after their own, train young people and keep the community together, through proper apprenticeships and support for local firms rather than a big government scheme.
S4.think: Ten years still worries her, but she could see the family getting through: Mark could switch work early, the children would be grown or nearly, and she'd hope an old church still needs a skilled carpenter.
S4.do: Saves steadily, pays extra off the mortgage when possible and keeps working. Encourages Mark to find safer work within a couple of years and steers her children towards hands-on or caring work, while learning restoration from an older craftsman.
S4.feel: Anxious but steadier, with time to put things right.
S4.quote: I'd hope there's still some old church that needs a carpenter who knows what she's doing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she sees a path through family planning and a niche in restoration, learned the old way. She still wants local, apprenticeship-based solutions, not government schemes. Her children's choices are central to how she thinks about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take Mark's job and mine at the same time, and we'd have nothing to fall back on but family. What would help is work, not handouts: local firms getting support to keep people on, and proper apprenticeships for whatever new jobs there are, so people can stand on their own feet again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of us out here, the church is where people would turn first, before any government. If you want to know how people would get through, ask the vicar, he'd know more than any study.

headlineQuote: If you want to know how people would get through, ask the vicar, he'd know more than any study.
portrait: Elena Schmidt is a 43-year-old carpenter for a small family builder in farming country, trained by her father, church-going, with a lorry-driver partner and two children. She has never used AI and doesn't plan to. AI Plateau leaves her grateful, while Steady Disruption makes her worry more about her partner's job than her own. AGI by 2028 alarms her because both incomes would go at once, and she'd lean on family, her brother's farm and the church. With five or ten years she saves hard, steers her children towards hands-on or caring work, and hopes old churches will still need her skills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take her job and her partner's at the same time with nothing to fall back on but family.
whatWouldHelp: Support for local firms to keep people on and proper apprenticeships for new jobs, so people can stand on their own feet rather than relying on handouts.
